pack.name: Business Law
pack.title: The Fine Print
pack.blurb: Courts, contracts, torts, statutes, landmark cases and the shapes a business can take.

prompts.text: Name an area or branch of law.
prompts.flavor: There is a law for everything. Somewhere there is a law about this.
prompts.rules: Any recognised field of legal study or practice.

answers.lore: Founded on the Outer Space Treaty of 1967: no nation may claim the Moon, and astronauts are to be treated as "envoys of mankind".
The customs medieval traders carried from fair to fair, enforced by their own courts on the spot, "between tides". Much of modern commercial law grew from it.

traps.reason: A law, in a manner of speaking, but no court will hear it.

prompts.text: Name a type of business structure or organisation.
prompts.flavor: A company is a person who cannot die and cannot be imprisoned. Think about that for a moment.
prompts.rules: Any legal form a business or organisation can take, in Australia or overseas.

answers.lore: A structure found almost nowhere but Australia, and only for mining. Shareholders who stop paying calls on their shares simply forfeit them, and owe nothing.
Investors pool their money and share the income. As each dies, the survivors' shares grow, and the last one alive takes all. Often banned, for the obvious reason.
A company with exactly one member, who is whoever holds a certain office. The Crown is one. So is an archbishop.

traps.reason: A place or a general word. Name the legal structure behind it.
Part of running one, but not a structure in itself.

prompts.text: Name a tort or a crime.
prompts.flavor: Every wrong has a name. Some have two, depending on who is suing.
prompts.rules: Any civil wrong or criminal offence known to the law, old or new.

answers.lore: Letting a company die with its debts, then rising the next morning as a new one with the same assets, the same staff and nothing owing.
An old English offence: being a quarrelsome nuisance to the neighbours. The punishment was the ducking stool. A New Jersey woman was charged with it as late as 1972.
Trying to sway a juror with bribes, threats or even persuasion. It was a common law crime for centuries, until bribery laws quietly took over its work.

traps.reason: Poor form, but not in itself a tort or a crime here.

prompts.text: Name a term from contract law.
prompts.flavor: Read every word before you sign. The oldest stories all turn on a clause somebody skipped.
prompts.rules: Any element, doctrine, remedy, clause or kind of contract.

answers.lore: "It is not my deed." The plea of someone who signed a document that was utterly different from what they believed it to be. It almost never works.
The seller stays the owner until paid. Named for a 1976 case over Dutch aluminium foil, which put the name Romalpa into every supply contract.

traps.reason: Around the contract, not in it.
That is the subject. Name a term from it.

prompts.flavor: All rise. Something is about to be decided, and it will stay decided.
prompts.rules: Any court, tribunal or commission that hears disputes, in Australia or elsewhere, past or present.

aliases: Supreme Court of New South Wales

answers.answer: Supreme Court of the United States

aliases: Judicial Committee of the Privy Council

answers.lore: A sham court. Oddly, the phrase is American, not Australian: it first appears in print in the United States in the 1840s and 1850s.

aliases: Court of Justice of the European Union

answers.answer: Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea

aliases: African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights

answers.lore: A medieval court held at fairs, named for the "pieds poudrés", the dusty feet of travelling traders. It gave judgment within a day. Bristol's sat until 1870.
England's court for disputes over coats of arms. It sat in 1954 for the first time in over two centuries, to rule on a theatre's use of Manchester's arms.

traps.reason: Part of the system, but nobody sits in judgment there.
Which court? Name it. The tennis kind does not count.

prompts.text: Name an Act of Parliament or other famous law.
prompts.flavor: Somebody stood up in a chamber and read it aloud three times. After that, it bound everyone.
prompts.rules: Any statute, code or founding legal document, Australian or foreign. The year is optional.

aliases: A New Tax System (Goods and Services Tax) Act
Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities
Australian Securities and Investments Commission Act

answers.answer: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act
Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act

answers.lore: The world's first copyright law, in force from 1710. It gave authors, not printers, the right to their work, for 14 years.
Passed in 1720, at the height of the South Sea mania, to stop new companies forming without a royal charter. It held British business back for a century.
The oldest law code yet found, written in Sumerian about 2100 BC, three centuries before Hammurabi. Unlike his, it mostly prefers fines to mutilation.

traps.reason: A court decision, not an Act. Judges made that one.

prompts.flavor: Two names with a small letter v between them. One of them lost, and became famous anyway.
prompts.rules: Any famous decided case, Australian or foreign, by its full or its popular name.

aliases: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Company
Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd
Amalgamated Society of Engineers v Adelaide Steamship
Dobbs v Jackson Women's Health Organization
Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v Boots Cash Chemists

answers.answer: Central London Property Trust v High Trees House
Commercial Bank of Australia v Amadio

aliases: Codelfa Construction v State Rail Authority

answers.lore: Nestlé sold records for cash plus three chocolate wrappers, which it then threw away. The House of Lords held in 1959 that even rubbish can be good consideration.
Two ships called Peerless sailed from Bombay, months apart. Buyer and seller each meant a different one. The court found there had never been a contract at all.

answers.answer: Burnie Port Authority v General Jones
Esanda Finance v Peat Marwick Hungerfords
Sharma v Minister for the Environment

answers.lore: A butcher from Wagga Wagga claimed in 1866 to be a lost English baronet. The heir's mother believed him. After two of England's longest trials, he got 14 years.

traps.reason: A court you watched rather than one that sat. Although the vibe was right.

prompts.text: Name a person or role you would find in a courtroom or the legal system.
prompts.flavor: Everyone in the room has a part and a place to stand. One of them would rather be elsewhere.
prompts.rules: Any job, office or role in a court or in the practice of law.

answers.lore: A judge's attendant in New South Wales and Victoria, named for the metal-tipped staff the office once carried, which was hollow to hold a warrant.
Someone who sits beside a person with no lawyer, to take notes and quietly advise. Named for a 1970 divorce case in which an Australian barrister was turned away.

traps.reason: A thing in the courtroom, not a person. And Australian judges do not use gavels.
